item.description:
Ben’s view National election days in the United States of America are biennial festivals of noise over signal. This is the day of maximal public attention to television and online news, on par with wars and natural disasters and the World Cup finals. Hundreds of millions of people are watching TV and YouTube closely, chattering and analyzing on social media. Media companies — like ours — will be there to keep you company, of course, in our case with superb analysis and a thoughtful afternoon livestream . item.title: Gas on the ballot in US elections
item.description:
Tim’s view Today’s US election is a test of how much voters will want to punish the president for soaring gasoline and power prices. Energy costs are always an important factor in elections; gas prices are the only economic indicator displayed in big bold numbers at major intersections. But between the war in Iran and the data center power rush, there’s rarely been an election in which energy prices — and the policy decisions pushing them up, from the White House to local zoning boards — are so much in the headlines. The average gas price during US President Donald Trump’s two years back in office is the highest it’s ever been halfway through a presidency, according to a Financial Times analysis. item.title: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
item.description:
The US said it will suspend South Africa and Rwanda from its free trade pact with sub-Saharan Africa, after months of fraying ties with both nations. Washington and Pretoria have repeatedly clashed since US President Donald Trump falsely accused South Africa of carrying out a genocide of its white population. Being dropped from the African Growth and Opportunity Act could cost South Africa — which already has one of the world’s highest unemployment rates — thousands of jobs. Meanwhile, Rwanda has faced Washington’s ire for supporting militias in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where US companies are seeking to ramp up mineral production. Experts warned the move could push the African countries closer to China , as it battles the US for influence on the continent. — Jeronimo Gonzalez
